mainEntity.name: What is a do-while loop in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: A do-while loop in Java is an exit-controlled loop that executes its body first and then checks the boolean condition. Because the condition is evaluated after the body, the loop body is guaranteed to execute at least once — regardless of whether the condition is true or false. Syntax: do { // body } while (condition); — the semicolon after the closing parenthesis is mandatory. Do-while loops are ideal for scenarios where you must perform an action before you can determine whether to repeat it, such as showing a menu and then checking if the user wants to continue, or reading input and then validating it.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between do-while and while loop in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: The fundamental difference is when the condition is evaluated. A while loop is entry-controlled — it checks the condition BEFORE executing the body. If the condition is false initially, the body never executes (0 or more executions). A do-while loop is exit-controlled — it executes the body FIRST, then checks the condition. The body always runs at least once even if the condition is initially false (1 or more executions). Syntax difference: do-while requires a semicolon after while(condition);. Use while when the body may not need to run at all. Use do-while when the body must execute at least once before the condition can meaningfully be evaluated.

mainEntity.name: When should you use a do-while loop in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use a do-while loop when: (1) The loop body must execute at least once before the condition is checked — for example, displaying a menu to the user before asking if they want to continue. (2) Input validation — read the input first, then validate it; keep repeating until valid input is entered. (3) Game loops — execute a game round at least once, then ask if the player wants to play again. (4) Retry logic — attempt an operation at least once, then decide based on the result whether to retry. If the body might not need to execute at all (condition could be false from the start), use a while loop instead.

mainEntity.name: Is the semicolon mandatory in do-while loop?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, the semicolon after the closing parenthesis of the while condition in a do-while loop is mandatory in Java. The correct syntax is: do { // body } while (condition); — without the semicolon, the code will not compile and will produce a compile-time error. This is the most common syntax mistake beginners make with do-while loops. The semicolon is what tells the compiler that the do-while statement has ended. This distinguishes it from a regular while loop which does not have a semicolon after its condition.

mainEntity.name: Can a do-while loop be replaced by a while loop?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, any do-while loop can be replaced by a while loop, but it requires duplicating the loop body before the while. For example: do { body; } while(condition); is equivalent to: body; while(condition) { body; }. This duplication of the body is error-prone and harder to maintain — if the body logic changes, it must be updated in two places. The do-while loop eliminates this duplication cleanly by guaranteeing one execution before condition evaluation. So while technically replaceable, the do-while loop is the more readable, maintainable choice when at-least-once execution is required.

sections.title: What is a Do-While Loop in Java?

blocks.text: A do-while loop in Java is an exit-controlled loop — it executes its body first and then evaluates the boolean condition. This is the fundamental difference from the while loop, which checks the condition before executing the body. Because the condition is evaluated after the body, a do-while loop always executes its body at least once — regardless of whether the condition is initially true or false.

Java provides three loop types: for (known iteration count), while (condition checked before body — entry-controlled), and do-while (body executes first — exit-controlled). The do-while loop is the least commonly used of the three, but it is the most natural fit for specific real-world patterns — especially menu-driven programs, input validation, game loops, and retry logic — where the action must happen before you can decide whether to repeat.

A critical syntax rule: the do-while statement must end with a semicolon after the closing while(condition). Forgetting this semicolon is the most common compile-time mistake with do-while loops. Unlike while and for, the do-while loop is the only loop in Java that requires a semicolon to terminate the statement.

blocks.title: 🔑 Java Do-While Loop at a Glance
blocks.text: do-while is exit-controlled — condition is checked AFTER the body. Body always executes at least once — even if condition is initially false. Semicolon after while(condition); is mandatory — forgetting it is a compile error. Best use cases: input validation, menu programs, game loops, retry logic. break exits the loop immediately from inside the body. continue skips the rest of the current iteration and goes back to the condition check. Nested do-while: valid but keep complexity manageable.

The do-while loop syntax is straightforward but has one critical difference from all other Java loops — the condition appears at the end, after the body. The body is wrapped in do { } and the condition follows in while(condition);. The semicolon at the end is non-optional.

items.title: Do-While Syntax
Execution Flow — Step by Step
items.text: Step 1: Execute the loop body (runs unconditionally the first time). Step 2: Execute the update statement (inside body — e.g., i++). Step 3: Evaluate the condition. Step 4: If condition is TRUE — go back to Step 1 (repeat). Step 5: If condition is FALSE — exit the loop; continue with the next statement. Key insight: Step 1 always happens regardless of the condition. The condition only controls whether to REPEAT — not whether to START.

items.title: Do-While vs While — The Critical Difference
items.text: while: checks condition → (if true) executes body → repeats. If condition is false initially, body NEVER runs. do-while: executes body → checks condition → (if true) repeats. Body ALWAYS runs at least once. Analogy: while is like 'check if it's raining before going outside.' do-while is like 'go outside first, then decide if you should come back in.' When the first action is mandatory regardless of the condition — use do-while.

sections.title: Input Validation with Do-While — The Classic Pattern

blocks.text: Input validation is the most common real-world use case for the do-while loop. The pattern is: read input first, then check if it is valid; if not valid, ask again. This is a perfect fit for do-while because you must read input at least once before you can evaluate it. Using a while loop for this requires duplicating the read statement — once before the loop and once inside.

items.title: Why Do-While Is Perfect for Input Validation
items.text: Input validation has a natural 'execute first, then decide' structure: you cannot know if input is valid before reading it. A while loop forces you to prime the pump — read before the loop just to check the condition, then read again inside. This duplication is error-prone. A do-while reads exactly once per iteration, checks validity after, and repeats only when necessary. The logic is in one place, the code is DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself), and the flow matches the natural thought process.

items.title: What to Validate
items.text: Common validation scenarios for do-while: numeric range (age 1–120, percentage 0–100, quantity > 0), string format (non-blank name, valid email pattern, password strength), menu choice (valid option from a list), PIN/OTP (correct value within limited attempts), date input (valid day/month/year), and yes/no prompts (must be 'Y' or 'N'). In all these cases, the input must be read before it can be validated — making do-while the appropriate loop.

items.title: Handling Scanner with Do-While
items.text: When using Scanner for input validation, be careful with nextInt() and nextLine() mixing — nextInt() does not consume the newline, causing nextLine() to return empty on the next call. Fix: call sc.nextLine() after sc.nextInt() to consume the leftover newline. Also, wrap nextInt() in a try-catch for InputMismatchException when the user types non-numeric input, and call sc.nextLine() in the catch block to clear the invalid token from the scanner buffer before the next iteration.

sections.title: Break and Continue in Do-While Loop

blocks.text: break and continue work inside do-while loops just as they do in while and for loops — but their interaction with the do-while's exit-controlled nature has subtle implications worth understanding. break exits the loop before the condition is even checked. continue skips the rest of the body and jumps directly to the condition check.

items.title: break in Do-While
items.text: break exits the do-while loop immediately, before the while condition is evaluated. This means the guaranteed 'at least once' execution can be cut short mid-body if break is hit on the first iteration. Use break in do-while for: early exit when a target is found, max attempt limits (e.g., 3 PIN attempts), error conditions that require immediate loop termination, and user cancellation mid-session. After break, execution resumes at the statement immediately after the closing while(condition);

items.title: continue in Do-While
items.text: continue in a do-while loop skips the remaining statements in the current iteration body and jumps directly to the while(condition) check. If the condition is true, the body executes again from the top. If false, the loop exits. Critical difference from while loop: in a while loop, continue jumps to the condition at the top; in a do-while loop, continue jumps to the condition at the bottom — the update logic must still be before the continue or after (depending on design) to avoid unintended infinite loops.

items.title: break vs continue in Do-While — Quick Guide
items.text: break: 'I'm done with the entire loop — exit now, skip condition check.' continue: 'I'm done with this iteration — check the condition and decide whether to run the body again.' In a do-while with a max-attempt PIN validation: use continue to skip printing when input is correct; use break to exit immediately upon success or when max attempts are exhausted. Always ensure the loop control variable is updated correctly before continue — otherwise the condition may never change and the loop runs forever.

blocks.title: ⚠️ continue in Do-While — Always Update Before continue
blocks.text: In a do-while loop, when you use continue to skip an iteration, make sure the loop control variable is updated BEFORE the continue statement — otherwise the condition at the bottom may never change, creating an infinite loop. Example of the bug: do { if(condition) continue; j++; } while(j < 10); — if continue fires, j++ is skipped and j stays the same forever. Fix: move j++ before the continue: do { j++; if(condition) continue; ... } while(j < 10). This is the same issue as in while loops but deserves special attention because the update is typically at the bottom of the do-while body.

Just like while and for loops, do-while loops can be nested — placing one do-while inside another. The inner loop executes completely for each iteration of the outer loop. Nested do-while loops are useful for 2D patterns, tabular data, and scenarios where both outer and inner iterations must execute at least once.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Nested Do-While — Reset Inner Variables
blocks.text: The most common nested loop bug is forgetting to reset the inner loop's control variable at the start of each outer iteration. In a do-while, initialization of the inner variable must happen inside the outer loop body (before the inner do-while begins) — not before the outer loop. Otherwise the inner loop's variable retains its final value from the previous outer iteration, causing the inner loop to not execute correctly (or not at all if the condition is already false). Always declare and initialize inner loop variables immediately before the inner loop begins.

sections.title: Bad Practices & Anti-Patterns — What Senior Developers Reject

blocks.text: These anti-patterns represent common misuses of do-while loops in professional Java code. Each one either causes bugs, hurts readability, or makes code harder to maintain and test.

items.title: Using Do-While When While Is Clearer
items.text: Reaching for do-while when a while loop is the natural fit makes code harder to understand. If there is any chance the body should not execute at all (e.g., iterating an empty collection, checking a condition that may be false from the start), use while. Do-while signals a specific contract to readers: 'this body always runs at least once.' Using it unnecessarily breaks that semantic expectation and confuses maintainers. Reserve do-while for cases where at-least-once execution is a genuine requirement.

items.title: Skipping Curly Braces
items.text: Java syntax technically allows a do-while with a single statement without braces: do System.out.println(x++); while(x < 5); — but this is dangerous and universally rejected in professional code. Adding a second statement below the do keyword while thinking it is inside the body is a silent logic bug. Always use curly braces for all do-while bodies, even single-statement ones. Every major Java style guide (Google, Oracle) mandates braces. The saved keystrokes are not worth the maintenance risk.

items.title: Complex Logic Inside the While Condition
items.text: Putting complex expressions in the while(condition) at the bottom of a do-while — especially expressions with side effects like method calls — makes the condition hard to reason about: do { ... } while (scanner.nextInt() > 0 && attempt++ < 3 && !isTimeout()); — the condition does too many things. Keep the while condition simple and boolean. Move side effects (reads, increments, method calls with consequences) into the body where they are visible and traceable. The while condition should express only the continuation criterion.

items.title: Using Do-While for Collections / Arrays
items.text: Do-while is not appropriate for iterating arrays or collections because it always processes the first element regardless of whether the collection is empty. If the array is empty, arr[0] in the body causes an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. For collections and arrays, always use a for-each loop or a for loop with a bounds check — both correctly handle the empty case by not executing the body at all. Do-while should never be the first choice for data structure iteration.

items.title: Deeply Nested Do-While Without Extraction
items.text: Three or more levels of nested do-while loops create code that is nearly impossible to read, debug, and test. It is a strong signal to refactor: extract inner loops into separate methods with descriptive names, replace nested loops with data structures (HashMap, Stream) where applicable, or break the problem into smaller composable functions. Deep nesting is both a complexity smell and a performance warning — triple-nested do-while over n elements is O(n³).

items.title: Hardcoding Magic Numbers in Loop Conditions
items.text: Writing do { ... } while (attempt < 3); scatters the literal 3 as a magic number. If the business rule changes to 5 attempts, every such literal must be found and updated — a maintenance risk. Define named constants: private static final int MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3; then use: do { ... } while (attempt < MAX_ATTEMPTS); This makes the intent clear ('max attempt limit') and the update trivial (change one constant). SonarQube and other static analysis tools flag magic numbers as a code quality issue.

sections.title: Java Do-While Loop Interview Questions — Beginner to Advanced

blocks.text: Do-while questions test your understanding of exit-controlled loops, the at-least-once guarantee, and the differences from while and for loops. These appear frequently in Java interviews at all levels.

items.q: Q1. What is a do-while loop in Java? How is it different from a while loop?
items.a: A do-while loop is an exit-controlled loop — the body executes FIRST, then the condition is evaluated. The body is guaranteed to execute at least once, even if the condition is initially false. A while loop is entry-controlled — the condition is checked BEFORE the body. If the condition is false initially, the body never executes. Syntax difference: do-while requires a mandatory semicolon after while(condition);. Use do-while when the body must always execute at least once (menus, input validation, retries). Use while when the body may not need to execute at all.

items.q: Q2. Is the semicolon after the while condition in a do-while mandatory?
items.a: Yes — the semicolon is mandatory and its absence is a compile-time error. The correct syntax is: do { // body } while (condition); — the semicolon tells the Java compiler that the do-while statement has ended. This is unique among Java loops — for and while do not end with a semicolon after their condition. Forgetting the semicolon is the single most common syntax mistake made by beginners with do-while loops. The compiler error message 'expected ;' will point directly to the missing semicolon.

Output: 10, then Final: 11. Even though i=10 makes the condition i<5 immediately false, the do-while body executes once first (prints 10, increments i to 11). Then the condition 11<5 is evaluated — it's false — so the loop exits. The final println prints 11. This is the key 'gotcha' for do-while: the body always runs at least once regardless of the condition. A while(i<5) loop would never execute the body and i would remain 10.

items.q: Q4. When would you use a do-while loop over a while loop?
items.a: Use do-while when: (1) The body must execute at least once before the condition can be meaningfully evaluated — for example, you cannot validate input before reading it. (2) Menu-driven programs — the menu must show before the user can choose to exit. (3) Game loops — a game round must play at least once before asking to replay. (4) Retry logic — an operation must be attempted at least once before checking for success or failure. (5) Digit operations on numbers — a number always has at least one digit (e.g., digit sum, digit count). If the body might need to be skipped entirely on the first check, use while.

items.q: Q5. Can a do-while loop be replaced by a while loop? Show an example.
items.a: Yes — any do-while can be replaced by a while, but it requires duplicating the body: do { body; } while(condition); is equivalent to: body; while(condition) { body; }. Example: do { int n = sc.nextInt(); } while(n <= 0); becomes: int n = sc.nextInt(); while(n <= 0) { n = sc.nextInt(); } — the input reading is duplicated. This duplication is error-prone (two places to update if logic changes) and is exactly why do-while exists. The do-while is cleaner, DRY, and more readable for at-least-once patterns.

items.q: Q6. What happens if you use continue in a do-while loop without updating the loop variable before it?
items.a: It creates an infinite loop. In a do-while loop, continue skips the remaining body statements and jumps directly to the while(condition) check. If the loop control variable is only updated after the continue statement, it never gets updated for iterations where continue fires. The condition never changes, remains true forever, and the loop runs infinitely. Fix: always update the loop variable BEFORE the continue statement. Example bug: do { if(x%2==0) continue; x++; } while(x<10); — for even x, continue fires, x++ is skipped, x stays even forever. Fix: do { x++; if(x%2==0) continue; ... } while(x<10);

items.q: Q7. Write a do-while loop to find the sum of digits of any number including 0.

items.a: Output: 10 20 40 80 160 160. Trace: x=5 → body: x=10, print 10. Condition: 10<100 true. x=10 → body: x=20, print 20. Condition: 20<100 true. x=20 → body: x=40, print 40. Condition: 40<100 true. x=40 → body: x=80, print 80. Condition: 80<100 true. x=80 → body: x=160, print 160. Condition: 160<100 false — exit. Then System.out.println(x) prints 160 on a new line. So the full output is: 10 20 40 80 160 on one line, then 160 on the next line.

items.q: Q9. Why is do-while preferred for menu-driven programs?
items.a: Menu-driven programs have a natural 'show first, decide later' structure: (1) Display the menu. (2) Get user choice. (3) Process the choice. (4) Ask if the user wants to continue. This is exactly the exit-controlled pattern — the menu must display at least once before any condition (user's exit choice) can be evaluated. Using a while loop requires either: duplicating the menu display before the loop and inside it, or using an awkward boolean flag initialized to true. Do-while eliminates duplication cleanly: the menu body is written once, runs at least once, and repeats only if the user doesn't choose exit. The resulting code is DRY, readable, and intent-revealing.

sections.title: Conclusion — Do-While: The Exit-Controlled Loop with a Guarantee

blocks.text: The do-while loop is Java's most purpose-specific loop — it exists precisely for scenarios where the body must execute at least once before the condition can be evaluated. While it is the least commonly used of Java's three loops, it is the most correct and most readable choice when that at-least-once guarantee is genuinely needed.

Mastering do-while means knowing not just its syntax — the mandatory semicolon, the body-first execution, the bottom condition — but also its appropriate use cases: input validation, menu-driven programs, retry logic, game loops, and digit operations. Equally important is knowing when not to use it — for collection iteration, when the body may need to be skipped, or when a while or for loop expresses intent more clearly. Choosing the right loop type is a mark of an experienced Java developer.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions — Java Do While Loop

items.q: What is a do-while loop in Java?
items.a: A do-while loop in Java is an exit-controlled loop that executes its body first, then evaluates the boolean condition. Because the condition is checked after the body, the loop body is guaranteed to run at least once regardless of the condition's initial value. Syntax: do { // body } while (condition); — the semicolon after the closing parenthesis is mandatory. It is ideal for input validation, menu programs, game loops, and retry logic where the action must occur before the condition can be meaningfully checked.

items.q: What is the difference between while and do-while loop?
items.a: while is entry-controlled — checks the condition BEFORE executing the body. If the condition is false initially, the body never runs (0 or more executions). do-while is exit-controlled — executes the body FIRST, then checks the condition. The body always runs at least once even if the condition is initially false (1 or more executions). Syntax: do-while requires a mandatory semicolon after while(condition);. Use while when the body may not need to execute. Use do-while when the body must always execute at least once.

items.q: Is semicolon mandatory after while condition in do-while?
items.a: Yes — the semicolon is absolutely mandatory. The correct syntax is: do { // body } while (condition); Without the semicolon, the Java compiler produces a compile-time error: 'expected ;'. This is unique to do-while — no other Java loop requires a semicolon after its condition. It is the most common syntax mistake beginners make with do-while loops. Always remember: the semicolon terminates the do-while statement.

items.q: When should I use a do-while loop in Java?
items.a: Use do-while when the loop body must execute at least once before the condition is evaluated: (1) Input validation — must read input before checking if it is valid. (2) Menu-driven programs — must display the menu before the user can choose to exit. (3) Game loops — must play a round before asking to replay. (4) Retry logic — must attempt an operation before checking if it succeeded. (5) Digit operations on numbers — a number always has at least one digit. If the body might legitimately need to be skipped entirely on first check, use a while loop instead.

items.q: Can do-while loop be replaced by while loop?
items.a: Yes — technically any do-while can be replaced by a while loop, but it requires duplicating the body before the loop: do { body; } while(condition); becomes: body; while(condition) { body; }. This duplication is error-prone (must update logic in two places if it changes) and reduces readability. The do-while loop exists precisely to avoid this duplication for at-least-once patterns. So while they are functionally equivalent, do-while is the more readable, maintainable, and semantically correct choice when at-least-once execution is required.
